title: Compilation units and interfaces: hiding a representation with an .mli
body: Every `.ml` file is a *compilation unit*: a module named after the file, compiled separately and linked with the others. A file `bounded_stack.ml` defines the module `Bounded_stack`, and another file reaches it as `Bounded_stack.push`. Dune works out the order in which the units must be compiled, so you never write that order down.

A unit may have an interface file, `bounded_stack.mli`, which is the signature of the module. Without it, everything in the `.ml` is public, including the layout of its types. With it, only what the `.mli` lists is visible, and a type declared there as plain `type t` is abstract: other units can pass values of type `t` around but cannot look inside, build one by hand, or depend on how it is stored. That is the compile-time enforcement of a representation invariant.

In the toplevel the same ideas apply: `#use "file.ml"` loads a file as if typed in, while `#load` and `#require` bring in compiled units and libraries, and modules defined in the toplevel have no `.mli`, so nothing is hidden there. Keep the `.mli` small and documented, because it is the contract other code is allowed to depend on.
challenge: The starter's src/bounded_stack.mli exposes the record type, so leak/leak.ml compiles by reading `items` directly. Rewrite the .mli so `t` is abstract and each function carries a documentation comment. The leak must stop compiling while the app keeps building.
projectInstructions: Try `dune build --root . ./leak/leak.exe` (it compiles now) and `dune exec --root . app/main.exe`. Edit only src/bounded_stack.mli. After your change the first command must fail with an unbound record field and the second must still work.
question: What does declaring `type t` without a definition in an .mli do?
correct: It makes t abstract: other units can use values of type t but cannot see or construct its representation
wrong: It deletes the type from the compiled library
reasoning: The signature hides the definition, so the only way to build or inspect a t is through the functions the interface exports.
